Years ago I volunteered at the local Legal Aid as an intake person.. 
I talked to thousands of low income Lane county residents who had civil problems. It was terribly underfunded but did a great deal with very little. On the criminal side, if one is accused of robbing a bank, one is given a lawyer if poor. However, on the civil law side of things, if one is poor and needs to file for divorce or is being brought into court by an ex who has a lot of money and wants custody, one may end up bewildered and lose custody, without legal help. 
Many Lane county residents receive legal notices every day, but without legal help cannot file paperwork to reply. 
If I have one criticism of the legal aid system, it is that they tend to operate quietly, so the community often doesn't know the great work they do. Their funding should be doubled, not cut. 
Hugh Massengill, Eugene Oregon

One out of every 20 months it is expected that the estimate will be off by more than +/-32,800 jobs.

This happened to my parents - they bought in 1988 and a few years later were in the position of having the value of the house fall below the amount of the mortgage.  They couldn't sell it because it meant finding an extra $100k to pay to the bank on top of the selling price of the house.

Keep that in mind when you buy something that runs this quick - it only has to "correct" to where it was a year or two ago and you will be locked into a bad situation.

Grade-separated rail is the creme-de-la-creme of fast dwell times because it doesn't stop anywhere but stations, and trains with level floors to platforms, numerous wide doors, and prepayment allow for literally hundreds of people to board/alight in less than 30 seconds.

Most important habit to cultivate from the beginning: track your expenditures.. And be diligent about it i.e. do it for years, consistently. How else will you know how much you need to save for retirement?

Most financial facelift articles do this in a gross way but often (I think) neglect to list the expenditures that recur intermittently vs monthly: cars need replacing; electronics need upgrading; hearing aids as you age; furniture replacement; new roof. 

All these things have big expense tags but seldom are factored into regular monthly expenditures. Result: more $$ is spent than expected and you think somebody's got their hand in your wallet.

We consistently factor in $2,000-$3,000 more per month than our 'regular' expenses (taxes, food, utilities, clothing, etc) because on an annual or 3-5-year basis, that's what we will spend.

There's always something! Tracking expenses is an eye-opener and will surely show you exactly what you'll need in retirement to maintain your lifestyle.
